terms.definition: Durkheim's distinction between things set apart and forbidden (sacred) and ordinary things (profane).
terms.examiner: The basis of the functionalist definition of religion.

terms.definition: The shared norms, values and beliefs that bind a society together.
A belief system that attaches sacred qualities to the nation and its institutions.
terms.examiner: Bellah; used to show religious functions surviving in secular forms.

terms.definition: Marx's description of religion as easing the pain of exploitation while hiding its cause.
terms.examiner: Pair with false consciousness; criticise with examples of religion driving change.

terms.definition: A distorted view of reality that prevents people from seeing their true interests.
terms.examiner: A Marxist concept; say how religion produces it.

terms.definition: The justification of the existing social order and its inequalities.
terms.examiner: E.g. the divine right of kings; useful in Marxist and feminist arguments.

terms.definition: The feminist view that religion justifies and maintains male dominance.
terms.examiner: Evidence: exclusion of women from roles, sacred texts; counter with women's active choices to take part.

terms.definition: The view that religion maintains things as they are, supporting tradition and existing power.
terms.examiner: Set against the view of religion as a source of change (11.3).

terms.definition: Non-religious institutions or beliefs that perform the functions religion once performed.
terms.examiner: A criticism of functionalism: if others can perform the function, religion is not essential.

terms.definition: The use of religion to unite a community and defend its identity against an external threat.
terms.examiner: Bruce; evidence that religion can stay strong where it carries national identity.
